mcqs.question: In a shallow copy, why does modifying the clone's tag list also change the original's tag list?
options: Both objects' tags field reference the exact same List instance in memory
Java copies lists by value automatically
The clone() method was called twice by mistake
Lists are always immutable, so this can't actually happen
mcqs.explanation: Shallow copy duplicates the field itself but not what it points to, so both objects end up holding the same list reference — mutating it through either object is visible to both. Java collections are copied by reference, not by value, and lists are mutable by default, which is exactly what makes this bug possible.

mcqs.question: In the `RobotConfig.clone()` code, why is it safe to copy the `name` field with a plain assignment instead of building a new object for it?
options: Strings are always garbage collected before clone() returns
String is immutable in Java, so no code can mutate the shared value out from under either object
Assignment always creates a deep copy for any field type
name is a static field shared across all instances
mcqs.explanation: Immutability is what makes reference-sharing safe: since a `String`'s value can never change after creation, both objects can point at the same one with zero risk. Assignment doesn't deep-copy in general — that's exactly why `tags` needed explicit copying — and `name` here is a normal instance field, not static.

mcqs.question: A class's `clone()` was written correctly, then a new mutable `Map<String, String> metadata` field was added later without updating `clone()`. What happens?
options: The code fails to compile until clone() is updated
clone() automatically deep-copies any field added after it was written
metadata silently becomes a shared reference between clones, reintroducing shallow-copy bugs for that field only
mcqs.explanation: Deep copying is per-field and manual — a field `clone()` doesn't explicitly handle falls back to a shared reference, shallow-copy style, even if every other field is handled correctly. Nothing here fails to compile, `clone()` has no way to auto-detect new fields, and the original's mutability is unaffected.

mcqs.question: A configuration object is expensive to build (a network call) and its exact shape is only known once assembled at runtime through user customization. Which pattern fits best?
options: Factory Method, since it can vary which subclass gets built
Builder, since it can assemble complex objects step by step
A plain constructor, since runtime data can always be passed as arguments
Prototype — clone the already-built instance instead of repeating the expensive, hard-to-parameterize construction
mcqs.explanation: Prototype is the only option that avoids re-running expensive construction and doesn't require the configuration's shape to be known in advance — it just copies an instance that already exists. Factory Method and Builder both build fresh from parameters, and a plain constructor has the same problem plus none of the decoupling benefits.
